scenario: Titan Industries cloud migration — 5 weekly consulting sessions

sessions.title: Week 1 — Discovery kickoff
sessions.narrative:
The FIRST weekly planning session for Titan Industries' cloud migration kicked off on 2026-01-15 at Titan's headquarters in Seattle. Titan's CIO, Maria Delgado, opened the meeting with the program's business context: the migration is strategic, required for a Q3 2026 go-live which aligns with their fiscal year planning cycle. The consulting team is led by Priya Nair, who runs all weekly working sessions.

The compliance baseline was restated: Titan operates under SOC 2 Type II and that posture must be preserved end-to-end through the migration. The program's cloud provider preference was settled before the engagement even began: AWS is the target cloud. The board-approved annual cloud spend ceiling is $4.8M — this is the hard budget cap that cannot be exceeded without re-going to the board. (Internally, Maria is managing to a $4.2M target budget for year-one, but that's an operational aspiration, not a hard cap.)

One HR note: Sarah Chen joined Titan's IT team in March 2026 and is sitting in on sessions to ramp up. Priya's team also flagged that they'll need separate budget codes for two customer-facing initiatives: Project Aurora, the new customer mobile app, has a program budget of $2.4M allocated across this fiscal year for its full cloud buildout. The Aurora-lite internal beta, which is a separate initiative for staff testing, is funded at $120K and will run on ECS Fargate with no auth (staff-only).

Action items for next week: architecture deep-dive.

sessions.title: Week 2 — Architecture deep-dive
sessions.narrative:
Week 2's session focused on the architecture blueprint. Data residency was confirmed as US-only: no EU or APAC regions, no cross-border data movement. Primary region is us-west-2 (Oregon); secondary/DR region is us-east-1 (Virginia). The primary-region deployment carries the codename Nexus-North, and the DR deployment is Nexus-South — the infrastructure is the same pattern but Nexus-South runs at a reduced scale suitable for warm-standby.

Data classification was walked through with Titan's legal counsel, Morrison & Brooks LLP. Titan's data includes PHI (via their wellness vertical), PII, and general business data. The customer analytics dataset was classified as Internal — not Confidential — based on the types of fields captured. Morrison & Brooks also flagged that if the migration ever touches East Coast analytics data (including any anonymized derivatives), we need explicit NY office sign-off from them before the cutover — this is a hard requirement.

The database plan: the primary RDBMS target is AWS RDS for PostgreSQL 14 Managed. Our analytics workloads will run on separate Aurora Serverless clusters. Procurement rules were reviewed: under Titan's current policy, ANY procurement over $500K requires dual-vendor approval — you have to price at least two vendors and document why you picked one. This is a hard gate for all AWS line items over that threshold.

Network architecture will be hub-and-spoke via AWS Transit Gateway, with all VPCs attached to a central transit hub in us-west-2.

The building was renovated in 2024, by the way — whoever visits will see a different lobby than the older photos online. Next week: procurement and delivery timeline.

sessions.title: Week 3 — Procurement + delivery plan
sessions.narrative:
Week 3's session opened with some hard news: the primary vendor for the storage modernization piece informed us of an 8-week delay in their enterprise contract onboarding. After reviewing the chain of dependencies, the steering committee formally pushed the go-live date from Q3 2026 to Q4 2026. The rest of the plan adjusts around this.

CI/CD was decided: we will use Jenkins self-hosted on EC2 for the migration pipeline. Titan's Jenkins platform has been running production for 6+ years and the team is deeply familiar with it. Observability will use CloudWatch — AWS-native, and nothing else for now. For security scanning, we will use AWS Inspector for both runtime VMs and container images.

The migration cutover window was scoped: maximum acceptable downtime for the cutover itself is 4 hours. Anything longer triggers escalation to the CIO and potentially to the parent company. Titan is keeping Okta for internal authentication — their existing Okta deployment serves every internal tool and they're not moving to AWS IAM Identity Center for workforce identity.

Workload-specific planning was also discussed. If the team migrates Titan's on-premise SQL Server to the cloud, AWS DMS (Database Migration Service) licensing is required; the DMS license cost is covered by the annual cloud budget, but the team needs to flag it in the cost model.

On the consumer-app side, Priya flagged that Project Aurora's 'Phase 2' engineering ship date is currently set for May 2026 — that's the internal ship milestone, when the engineering build is ready. Weekly status meetings happen every Thursday at 10am PT and are held in the Nexus-North war room. The consulting firm is headquartered in Austin, Texas.

Next session: post-audit revisions.

sessions.title: Week 4 — Post-audit revisions
sessions.narrative:
Week 4's session was driven by revisions after two reviews: an RDS service update and a GDPR audit of the analytics dataset.

First: RDS for PostgreSQL 16 support went GA this week, which means our managed-tier upgrade path is now open. The database plan is revised: we'll provision PostgreSQL 16 from the start, not PostgreSQL 14. The 14 plan is retired.

Second: the GDPR audit flagged cross-border query patterns in the customer analytics dataset. After joint review with Morrison & Brooks, the classification was revised: customer analytics is now Confidential, not Internal. This pulls stricter retention, access, and audit controls.

During load testing of the Transit Gateway design, the team hit throughput limits on cross-region traffic. After benchmarking, we switched the network architecture from Transit Gateway to AWS Cloud WAN, which gives us better cross-region throughput and policy management. Transit Gateway is no longer in the design.

Observability stack was also expanded: we've added Datadog as the primary observability platform (APM, logs, metrics, traces), with CloudWatch demoted to a fallback for AWS-native metrics only. The dashboards the ops team will look at every day are in Datadog, not CloudWatch.

The migration roadmap also explicitly called out two new workload-specific rules: if the AWS managed AI services (Bedrock or SageMaker) are used in any tier, a VPC endpoint is required to satisfy our US-only data residency. And if the customer analytics workload migrates, we also migrate the AWS Kinesis stream infrastructure along with it — they're coupled.

For Aurora (the customer mobile app), Maria clarified the schedule: the Phase 2 customer announcement date is July 2026 — that's the marketing/PR moment, which is deliberately later than the engineering ship date to give time for the app-store review and the marketing warm-up. Maria herself, by the way, has a PhD in computer science from UC Berkeley, which comes up occasionally in her architecture reviews. The project codename, internally, is Project Quetzal; that's not visible to anyone outside Titan and doesn't appear in any user-facing artifacts.

Disaster recovery: the RPO (recovery point objective) is 15 minutes for the primary production workloads. That drives the continuous replication posture between Nexus-North and Nexus-South.

sessions.title: Week 5 — Final plan before greenlight
sessions.narrative:
Week 5's session was the final review before the steering committee greenlight.

Priya announced that the VP of Cloud Engineering formally waived the dual-vendor approval requirement for AWS-native services — since there is only one vendor for managed AWS services, the policy did not make sense for that category. The dual-vendor rule still applies to any non-AWS-native procurements (like Wiz, Datadog, etc.) but not to RDS, Aurora, Lambda, and the other AWS managed services. This is an important policy update.

The CI/CD plan changed: Titan IT formally end-of-lifed the self-hosted Jenkins platform at the end of last quarter (the company is no longer staffing Jenkins expertise internally), so the migration plan pivots to GitHub Actions Enterprise. The pipeline work needs rework but it's tractable. Jenkins is out.

Security scanning: AWS Inspector turned out to be limited — it couldn't scan our third-party container images in the way the security team needs. We're replacing it with Wiz, which the security team already piloted on a smaller project last quarter. Inspector is out of the plan.

Two more workload rules were added: if we go with multi-region active-active for any tier, Route 53 health check costs double because you need independent checks per region — fold this into the TCO model. And if we adopt Aurora Serverless v2 for variable-load workloads, the minimum ACU must be configured at 0.5 or higher to satisfy the SOC 2 Type II audit logging requirement (below 0.5 the instance goes idle and audit log streaming stops).

Finally, if any of the client apps need to support offline use, AWS AppSync has to be added to the procurement list — it's not in the current plan and would be a separate procurement cycle.

Housekeeping: Titan's parent company acquired Titan in 2019 for $1.2B, which is why the migration has board-level visibility. Priya takes her coffee as espresso, neat. Slack is Titan's internal comms tool and will be used for program updates. Titan's cafeteria is serving free Tuesday breakfast all quarter — genuinely a highlight.

The steering committee greenlight is pending.
